text: This chapter's lab combines everything just covered into one real scenario on the Problem table: a UI Action button and a scripted UI Policy, working together through a real relationship between two tables.

The scenario: build a Close All Related Tasks button, visible only when the Problem is Resolved and the user holds the itil role, that closes every open Incident linked to it. Pair that with a UI Policy that warns when more than three related Incidents exist. The two tables connect through problem_id on Incident, which stores the causing Problem's sys_id.

The UI Action's Condition field checks two things with an AND: current.state equals 6, Resolved on the Problem table, and gs.hasRole of itil. Both must be true before the button even renders - exactly the gating pattern the UI Actions lesson introduced.

With Client unchecked, the Script field runs server-side. It builds a GlideRecord against incident, filters on problem_id matching current.sys_id and active true, then loops with while next, setting each matching incident's state to Closed and calling update. action.setRedirectURL sends the user back to the Problem once every related incident has been closed.

The UI Policy's Run-scripts pair handles the earlier warning. Inside onCondition_true, g_form.getUniqueValue returns the Problem's own sys_id, which a fresh client-side GlideRecord query uses to count open related incidents. GlideRecord works here because the platform proxies it to the server and waits for the result - which is also exactly why it should be used sparingly, never in a tight loop. Past three related incidents, showFieldMsg displays a warning on the state field; onCondition_false clears it again once the condition is no longer true.

It would be tempting to put that same warning logic inside the UI Action instead, but that's the wrong tool - the UI Action only fires after a click, server-side, as a one-time action. It can't warn the user before they decide whether to click it in the first place. The UI Policy's job is exactly that earlier, live, client-side moment; the UI Action's job is the one-time, server-side mutation after the decision is made.
That closes Chapter 4. Next up, Chapter 5 begins Scoped Applications, starting with what an application scope actually protects.
